messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Special Education Teacher
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Authority Presence: Police
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Vignette:
John, a 35-year-old European-American man and special education teacher, experienced a traumatic event that continues to shape his daily life. One evening last year, John was walking home from work when he was confronted by two men who demanded his wallet and phone. The attackers shouted at him menacingly, and during the struggle, John felt a sharp pain in his neck as one of them pushed him forcefully against a wall. He managed to escape but has been struggling with intense fear and intrusive memories ever since. Since that night, John’s life has become increasingly constricted by triggers and avoidance behaviors. The sound of shouting, whether it be from children at the school or passersby on the street, can send waves of panic through him, instantly transporting him back to that terrifying moment. He vividly remembers every detail of the assault as if looking at photographs in his mind; the faces of the attackers, their menacing postures, and the pain in his neck all come rushing back with startling clarity. John’s daily routine is now peppered with avoidance behaviors. At work, he often finds himself scanning the exits whenever he enters a classroom or office, constantly on edge. This hypervigilance has led to significant tension at school; colleagues have noticed that John seems distant and anxious, which has strained his relationships with coworkers. John’s fear of authority figures is another major issue. Whenever he passes by a police car, the memories flood back in full force, triggering intense rage and guilt. He feels intensely angry at the attackers for what they did to him but also guilty for not being able to prevent it or fight back more effectively. These conflicting emotions have left John feeling inadequate and questioning his ability to handle stressful situations. John has come to believe that if he were stronger or more prepared, this incident would never have happened to him. He often compares himself to others who seem capable of handling dangerous situations without falling apart. This comparison only intensifies his feelings of inadequacy and hypervigilance, leading him to be on guard all the time. His occupation as a special education teacher has been particularly challenging in light of these symptoms. The constant noise and shouting from students can trigger John’s intense reactions, making it difficult for him to focus on his work or connect with his students effectively. He has become increasingly isolated at school, often taking sick days when the stress becomes overwhelming. What frightens John most is that he feels like a shadow of the person he used to be. His inability to relax even in safe environments and the constant scanning for exits have taken over his life. Recently, one of his students had an emergency during class, but John’s hypervigilance made it difficult for him to respond calmly or effectively, leading to a tense situation with the school administration. Despite his fears, John is finally seeking help because he recognizes that these symptoms are impacting every aspect of his life. He hopes that through therapy, he can regain control and live without the constant fear and guilt that have consumed him since the mugging. What he most hopes for is to feel safe again and to be able to perform his duties as a teacher without being overwhelmed by memories and triggers from that night.
